## Part 2 · 10:09

[10:09] So, I'm not an expert in this area, but in my studies we we learned about either classical theism or neo-classical theism. So, classical theism would make strong stand on that to say God doesn't he is outside of time, so he's timeless and he creates everything in one timeless moment. So, all of his actions are actually identical to each other, all of his attributes are identical to each other and he doesn't go from one state to another, he just is. Um, and neo-classical theists would go, "No, actually look, scripture seems to say like God becomes the creator of the world.

[10:39] He becomes the father of Abraham. He becomes the father of Isaac. He is grieved when we sin. The Holy Spirit is grieved when we sin. He regrets. He experiences regret at having made mankind." Um, and so neo-classical theists would say, "You know, we we're going to keep the essential attributes of God, his omnipotence, his omnipresence, his uh, uh, uh, um, all all of these essential attributes, but we're going to, you know, put an asterisk on some of these other claims about his simplicity or his uh, immutability.

[11:16] We're going to say he's unchangeable in his essential nature, but he does go through a change from one state to another and there are many Christians who throughout history have held to that and it doesn't make you not a Christian to hold to those things. >> Right.
